howto: Play the lesson and follow along. The line being spoken is highlighted; tap any line to jump to it.
When you see Your turn, say the phrase out loud in a full voice before the answer comes. Don't wait for it.
Hide the Maya spelling once a phrase feels familiar. Reading is a crutch; the goal is hearing and speaking.
Finish the lesson at the bottom of the transcript and tick anything you blanked on. Those phrases come back sooner in the next lessons.

sounds.d: Glottalized. Said with a sharp pop from the throat, like a small cough on the consonant. k' versus k changes the word.
A glottal stop on its own, a catch in the throat like the middle of uh-oh. Very common at the ends of words.
Long vowels, held about twice as long as a single vowel, with a low, level pitch.
Long vowels with a high, falling pitch. Yucatec Maya is tonal: sáamal and saamal are different words.
A vowel cut off by a glottal stop, often re-articulated: a-'a.
A breathy h, as in Spanish jamón.
As in English cats, at the start of a word.
As in English water. Appears before vowels after in, a, u: in wíits'in.

patterns.d: My, your, his or her. They go in front of the word: in k'aaba', my name; a beel, your road; u yotoch, his house.
Táan marks something happening right now. Táan in bin, I'm going. Táan a bin, you're going.
Then, or so. Ends many sentences: Ma'alob túun, alright then.
Until. Tak sáamal, until tomorrow. Tak tu jeel k'iin, until another day.
How. Bix a beel, how is your road, how are you. Bix a k'aaba', how is your name, what's your name.

spelling: Spelling follows the 2014 INALI standard used across the Yucatán Peninsula. Older books use colonial spellings (c for k, dz for ts', cħ for ch'); the sounds are the same.
